9.author: St. Cyprian of Carthage
9.text: Cyprian's third-century treatise on the Lord's Prayer is the earliest extant Christian commentary on it. He notices first the boldness of the address: Father. No Old Testament prayer dared this. Christ has given us the word, Cyprian says, because He has first made us sons. We do not call God Father by nature, as the Son does; we call Him Father by adoption, and the very fact that the word is ours is the whole gospel in miniature. The rest of the petitions only unfold what it means to live as children of such a Father.

9.author: St. Gregory of Nyssa
9.text: Gregory of Nyssa observes that the prayer Christ teaches has no first-person singular. There is no 'my Father, give me my daily bread, forgive me my debts.' Every petition is plural. The Christian who prays the Our Father has already been baptized into a body; he prays for himself only inasmuch as he prays for all. To ask anything else would be to learn from Christ a prayer that contradicts Him.

33.author: St. Maximus the Confessor
33.work: Four Hundred Chapters on Love, II
33.text: Maximus the Confessor takes Christ's command 'seek first the Kingdom' as the rule for the whole of Christian asceticism. He distinguishes the two kinds of seeking: the natural cares that fix the mind on food, clothing, and shelter, and the higher seeking that fixes the mind on God. Christ does not condemn the first; He orders the second. The Christian who has put the Kingdom first will find the necessities of the body added by God's providence, not because anxiety produces them but because the Father who feeds the birds does not forget His own children.
